Introduction - July 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

In last month’s issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, we noted the decline in base metal prices, which pushed the GFMS Base Metal Index down to 231.84 in early June, some 22% below the high for this year.  Since then, the base metals complex has recovered somewhat with our index rising to over 250 in early July. 

A month ago, a key factor for the market were concerns about the deepening financial crisis in some of the Mediterranean economies.  Since then, the focus has shift

ed towards the potential for slower demand growth within the key consuming regions of the EU, North America, and perhaps most importantly China. In addition to these cyclical economic concerns, the markets are also beginning to respond to the pronounced seasonal lull in demand in the northern hemisphere markets. ###### **Price declines are not yet sufficient to trigger a supply** ###### **response** Importantly, despite the decline in prices they generally remain above marginal production costs and we have not seen any significant cutbacks despite lower prices. Another area of concern (for producers) are the sharp gains in Chinese production (both at the concentrate level and to a slightly lesser extent the refined stage), which is in turn affecting China’s trade position, either turning the country into a net exporter of some metals, or leading to a reduction in the net import position. In addition to higher Chinese production on the base metals, there are growing concerns about the rate of Chinese economic growth going forward, which are discussed in the Economics section (E2). There are also increasing concerns about the prospects for growth in the mature economies as governments implement measures to rein the huge fiscal deficits that have been accumulated. ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

###### **Underlying base metal demand remains firm (so far)** Despite these economic concerns, most of the data relating to non-ferrous semis output remains firmly in positive territory and our discussions with fabricators still point to an on-going recovery in operating rates downstream. This view is generally supported by the various statistics that have been released over the last month concerning orders and shipments for fabricated products. Although base metal prices have been under pressure, the trend in LME inventories remains broadly supportive for most of the metals. The changes are also broadly in line with our views on the wider fundamentals, with copper and tin stocks falling significantly. For nickel, where LME inventories have fallen by 15,000 tonnes over the last month and by over 40,000 tonnes from the high for the year seen in early February, GFMS expects that the downtrend may be reversed in the summer months as stainless producers curb output in response to excessive output in the first half of this year and lower alloy surcharges. For lead and zinc, the decline in LME stocks has been modest (partly due to the sharp rise in Chinese domestic production). However, we favour the underlying fundamentals of the lead market more than those for zinc. Aluminium inventories have fallen slightly, but they remain by far the largest in terms of num

ber of weeks consumption at above 10 weeks compared to just over 2 weeks for copper and lead. Although the majority of these stocks may not be immediately available to the market, their presence is likely to overhang the market, and aluminium prices should underperform the sector as a whole. ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

The closely-watched quarterly Tankan survey (June) showed a broad-based improvement in business. The diffusion index for large manufacturers improved to 1 in June from -14 in March, the first positive reading since June 2008, indicating the majority of large manufacturers viewed business conditions as favourable. The key concern going forward is whether export demand, which has primarily supported the Japanese economy, will be maintained. In China, the latest data for the main indicators such as industrial production and fixed asset investment suggest a marginal easing in the rate of economic growth within the country. IP grew by an estimated 16.5% in May down from 17.8% in April. Year-to-date industrial production has slowed each month since February, as investment and production naturally slips after the spike in 2009 and in response to gradual tightening measures from Chinese authorities. Year-to-date fixed asset investment slowed marginally in May, to 25.9% year-on-year down, which represents the eighth successive decline. Reduced bank lending and tighter credit conditions are limiting business investment, while infrastructure investment is starting to ease as government projects are completed. With this trend in place and with Chinese authorities actively working to cool growth amid emerging inflation pressures, fixed investment is expected to play a smaller part as a driver of economic activity later this year. However of greater concern to the base metals industry are the latest purchasing managers’ indices, with the government index falling to its lowest since February dipping to 52.1 in June from 53.9 in May. The HSBC PMI registered a weaker performance falling to 2 points to 50.4. Perhaps somewhat surprisingly, confidence in the Eurozone remained relatively unchanged in June with the economic sentiment index at 98.7, up from 98.4 in May. Nevertheless, we expect that this indicator will dip in the summer months due to concerns over the sustainability of the economic recovery, rising unemployment, and sovereign debt problems. At end-June, LME stocks stood at 449,425 tonnes and those at the Shanghai Futures Exchange at 123,939 tonnes, 33,759 tonnes and 26,150 tonnes down respectively on the end-May figures._** - **_Official Chinese production and trade flows data illustrates a declining apparent consumption against rising semis fabrication, suggesting excess supply in the country may well be on the decline and a near-balanced market is not out of sight._** - **_ICSG and WBMS data continues to suggest demand recovery in most mature markets lacks momentum, although the latest figures seem to overstate the weakness._** - **_We have scaled down our projections for quarterly price averages to reflect the lower starting point as well as the realisation by the mainstream that the recovery may be slower than originally expected. Although we continue to see prices breaching the $8,000/tonne mark before the end of the year, we no longer expect this to be done on a sustainable basis._** - **_Our supply-demand projections for the next twelve months remain unchanged from the previous edition of our Base Metals One Year Forecast and we continue to see the market move into deficit in the final quarter._** - **_Although our Base Case scenario paints a bright picture for copper prices going forward, we continue to ascribe significant probability to our bearish Scenario C. Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - July 2010 ###### **Market background** As we enter the second half of 2010, risk aversion continues to weigh on the copper price. Soon after the release of the previous edition of this report, prices plunged through the previously well defended $6,200/tonne mark to a low below $6,100/tonne, triggered by disappointing US jobs data, against the backdrop of ongoing concerns over debt levels of a number of European governments. Although prices have recovered since then, we have noticed strong resistance culminating in the $6,800s. More importantly, prices continue to be sensitive to bad news, which investors saw emerge across all key markets for the red metal. Indeed, GFMS would argue that the current sentiment towards copper (and pro-cyclical markets in general) mirrors that seen in the run-up to the year-to-date peak in early April, when risk appetite was growing rapidly and the consensus projections saw a relatively smooth path to global economic recovery. In this last point lies the key assumption for our broadly continued positive outlook towards copper prices. During the rally to (and briefly through) the $8,000/tonne mark we had cautioned that market conditions, although imp

roved, were far from able to support such price levels, particularly as these compared to marginal (95th percentile) costs of production in the $4,000s and that a correction was due. In a similar manner, we now feel that over the last few weeks, markets have tended to overestimate the risk of the sovereign debt crisis evolving into wide-spread defaults or restructuring. Moreover, although we have always tended to be sceptical towards the prospects of uninterrupted recovery for the global economy, we now feel that the potential impact of any “bumps” along the way will have on copper demand and, by implication, prices may be less dramatic than current investor sentiment seems to suggest. ###### **Persistent declines in LME inventories suggest relatively benign fundamentals** June was yet another month of decline for reported inventories. LME stocks fell by 26,150 tonnes over the month, to reach 449,425 tonnes, with an approximate 5,000 tonne outflow through to the time of publication. Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) stocks fell by 33,759 tonnes, to reach 123,939 tonnes by end-June. For some time now, GFMS have been sceptical towards the downtrend in reported inventories noted over the last few months. Rather than a market in deficit, we have tended to interpret these declines as suggestive of material flowing into unreported inventories in China, and we continue to believe this has been the case to some extent over the last few weeks. At the same time, we would reiterate our belief that these additions to unreported stocks are probably limited in magnitude. This is clearly illustrated in our quarterly supply-demand balances, which show only a modest surplus, averaging a little over 20,000 tonnes per month for the January-September period. Moreover, the reluctance of investors and other holders of such stocks to release this material into the market, even when prices stood around $8,000/tonne in early April, suggests a positive sentiment towards local consumption going forward. ###### **Latest Chinese data suggest oversupply is declining** The above contention that the additions to unreported stockpiles (in other words the surplus) over the last few months has been limited is supported by the latest data on Chinese production as well as copper trade flows. Apparent refined copper consumption (defined as the sum of production and net imports) stood at nearly 659,000 tonnes in May, whereas semis production, according to official statistics, stood at just over 897,000 tonnes. Importantly, the former has, for the last few months, trended downwards, whereas the latter has kept to an upward trajectory. (It is Copper Premiums Jan 05 - Present

It is worth noting here that, as one can see in the tables in the following pages, both organisations’ forecasts fall short of our projections. ###### **Blackout affects Zambian production** Around mid-June a nationwide blackout hit Zambia, as a result of a fault at a hydro power station, causing production in the country’s copper mines to halt. Electricity supply was restored within hours, meaning operations could be restarted within the same day. The loss of output for part of the day coupled with secondary effects, for instance the flooding of Vedanta’s Konkola mine and damages to electrical equipment at First Quantum’s Bwana Mkubwa, is expected to see June production fall short of targets. ###### **Collahuasi strike weighs on Chilean production** Official statistics showed Chilean copper production amounted to just under 431,000 tonnes in May, marking a 5.3% decline on the April figure and down 5.4% year-onyear. The decline was in large part the result of a strike by workers of the Collahuasi copper mine, which halted output at the operation for a number of days. Combined with increases earlier in the year, this saw total production over the January to May period rise by 1.3% year-on-year. It is interesting to note that in early June, Chile’s state commission, Cochilco, revised its forecast for the average copper price in 2010 to $3.20/lb ($7,055/tonne), compared to a previous projection of $3.10/lb, stating its belief that the euro-crisis and its adverse effects on the red metal’s price will prove temporary. **C4** 

Copper - July 2010 











Looking at the United States and China, the change in sentiment has if anything brought the consensus closer to our view, which had always been sceptical towards the uninterrupted recovery thesis.  At the same time, we cannot see growth turning negative in the former country and collapsing in the latter and, more importantly, we would be surprised if positive growth in copper consumption were not seen over the year. 

As a result of the above, our projections for copper supply and demand over the next twelve months have not been changed since the previous edition of our Base Metals One Year Forecast, and we still see the market swinging to deficit in the last four months of the year.  This is not the case for our price projections though.  Given the lower base and the breach of what we had previously expected to be a floor at $6,200/tonne, our revised projections for copper prices are more conservative. 

Although we continue to see a recovery in the second half of the year, we now expect that, although the $8,000/tonne barrier may well be breached before the end of the year, this is unlikely to be on a sustaina

ble basis and prices average $7,500/tonne over the final quarter. ###### **Market background** 

A semblance of reality has appeared to have returned to the nickel market with the LME cash quote trading a relatively narrow range of $17,955-20,505/tonne in June, compared to previous ranges of $21,050-25,650/tonne in May, and $24,400-27,600/tonne in April.  The average cash price in June was $19,389/tonne, 25.5% down from the high so far this year in April.  Part of the decline can be explained by the correction from the over-bought situation seen earlier in the second quarter, which saw prices peak at $27,600/tonne. 

However, from a fundamental standpoint, one key factor that has led to a correction in the price is lower offtake from the stainless steel sector.  This in turn reflects a number of key factors.  First, this is a reaction to the sharply higher levels of stainless output seen earlier this year.  As noted in the previous monthly issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, global stainless steel output increased by 54.6% year-on-year in the first quarter to 4.472 million tonnes. GFMS believes that higher operating rates were maintained for much of the second quarter, but that there was evidence of mills curbing output towards the end of this period. 

###### **Stainless will be a negative factor for nickel in the third quarter…** 

The nickel market also focused on the impending seasonal decline in stainless steel production in Europe, and the likely adverse impact of lower alloy surcharges.  European stainless mills have already announced a reduction in alloy surcharges for July for flat products with the surcharge for 304 material likely to be in a range of €1,600-1,700/tonne down from €1,800-1,900/tonne.  The likelihood of further reductions in the surcharge in the summer months has also put base prices for stainless steel under pressure, which currently stand at around €1,180/tonne compared to the recent high of €1,220/tonne (for 304 material). 

However, going somewhat against this trend is the announcement by Acerinox that it is set to work at near full capacity until the end of July due to its current

strong order flow. As a result, production is likely to return to pre-crisis levels of early 2008, with output around 600,000 tonnes in the second quarter. Nevertheless, we believe that orders could dry up as both consumers and service centres withdraw from the market in expectation of lower prices in August and September. **N2** Independent - Informed - International Nickel & Cobalt - July 2010 ###### **… as mills curb output** In the short term, demand for nickel will be hit by the overcapacity in the stainless steel sector, although from a longer term perspective for nickel demand this can be viewed as a positive for the industry, if it keeps stainless steel prices relatively low compared to other materials. The most obvious example of over-capacity is in China. This in turn is reflected in the stainless steel trade data, which has seen exports surge, albeit from a low base. The latest figures (for May) show exports up 30% month-on-month. ###### **China: A temporary bearish factor** The latest data on Chinese for nickel suggest that the upside for the metal will be capped during the summer months. China imported 10,719 tonnes of refined nickel in May, 36% lower than in April and 57% down year-on-year. Cumulative imports were down 4.8% at 75,222 tonnes. However, imports of nickel ore remain high, which in turn suggests that nickel pig iron production will remain at elevated levels. Although firm figures do not exist on actual production levels, GFMS believes that they are towards the high end of current estimates, with output more than doubling in the first five months of this year to over 70,000 tonnes. Given a nickel price of close to $20,000/tonne, and with high inventories of nickel ore within China, we continue to expect high operating rates from this source. ###### **Demand looks set to soften** Reflecting weaker demand, nickel premiums appear to have peaked in the North America (even before the resolution of the Vale dispute). In addition, more supply is coming to this market from various LME warehouses, attracted by the premium differential. Now that the strike at Vale has been resolved, we believe that the immediate focus of the market will return to the poor underlying demand conditions. We expect that demand sentiment in Europe will ease further in the coming months. Given the increasing uncertainty about the wider economic environment, and the more specific issues of ample availability of stainless steel, and the negative impact of alloy surcharges, all imposed on a pronounced seasonal slowdown, suggest that the nick

el market may come under some pressure in the short term. ###### **Supply growth is limited (short term)** In terms of nickel supply, production growth outside of China remains limited. This primarily reflects lower production at Vale’s strike-bound Canadian operations (now resolved) and the delays with the commissioning of the next generation of the PAL projects. According to the World Bureau of Metal Statistics, global refined nickel production increased by 5% in the first four months of this year. However, if you strip out the growth in Chinese production, output elsewhere in the world is generally lagging below last year’s levels. Production in both Europe and South Africa is largely unchanged, while the pending increase to South American production, mainly Brazil, will not affect the market to next year. The main source of the decline has, of course, been Canada reflecting the year-long-strike at Vale’s operations. Apart from the impending restart of these operations there have been few supply developments over the last month. Looking ahead, Talvivaara, the Finnish nickel producer, has recently secured financing to help finance at the mine. According to the company, volumes have increased from 628 tonnes in April to 808 tonnes in May and to over 1,200 tonnes in June. Eventually the project should have a capacity of around 50,000 tpy.
